Effect of organic compositions of aerobically pretreated municipal solid waste
on non-methane organic compound emissions during anaerobic degradation
Yuanyuan Zhang a, Dongbei Yue a,⇑, Jianguo Liu a, Liang He b, Yongfeng Nie a
a Key Laboratory for Solid Waste Management and Environment Safety, Ministry of Education of China, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
b BESG Environmental Engineering Co. Ltd., Beijing 100101, China
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 15 November 2011
Accepted 3 January 2012
Available online 14 February 2012
Keywords:
Non-methane organic compounds
Organic composition
Aerobically pretreated municipal solid
waste
Anaerobic degradation
a b s t r a c t
Odor pollution caused by municipal solid waste (MSW) treatment plants has become a growing public
concern. Although aerobic pretreatment of MSW has advantages in accelerating landﬁll stabilization,
the property of non-methane organic compound (NMOC) emissions from aerobically pretreated MSW
(APMSW) during landﬁlling is unknown. To investigate NMOC emissions from anaerobic degradation
of APMSW and to study the impact of organic compositions of APMSW and their decomposition stages,
ﬁve simulative anaerobic bioreactors (R1–R5) were ﬁlled up with APMSW of different original organic
compositions in a laboratory. For NMOC analysis, samples were collected from the gas that accumulated
separately during two successive independent stages of the whole experiment. The results showed that
the cumulative quantities of NMOCs from R1 to R5 were 1.11, 0.30, 0.18, 0.28, and 0.31 mg/kg DM,
respectively, when volatile solid was degraded by 34.8–47.2%. As the organic content of the original
waste was lower, the proportion of NMOCs generated in the early stage of anaerobic degradation became
higher. Multiple linear regression analyses of the relationship between the quantities of degraded organ-
ics and generated NMOCs showed that lipid and protein have a strong effect on NMOC amount. The effect
of lipid on NMOC quantity lasts longer than that of protein. This observation suggests that controlling the
lipid and protein contents in MSW can reduce the odor from landﬁlls.

1. Introduction
Conventional landﬁlling is a common method adopted world-
wide to dispose of municipal solid waste (MSW). During the anaer-
obic degradation of MSW, most organic matter is broken down by
microorganisms into simple compounds, leading to the formation
of landﬁll gas. CO2 and CH4 are the dominant components in land-
ﬁll gas. Trace species, such as mercury, arsenic, and some organic
compounds, are often found abundantly in landﬁll gas relative to
other environmental sources (Kim and Kim, 2002; Feng et al.,
2004; Huang et al., 2009). Although non-methane organic com-
pounds (NMOCs) comprise less than 1% (V/V) of landﬁll gas, they
may create a disproportionate environmental burden and potential
risk to human health (Allen et al., 1997). For example, emissions of
carcinogens, such as benzene and vinyl chloride, pose a potential
threat to workers and local inhabitants (El-Fadel et al., 1997;
Durmusoglu
et
al.,
2010).
Furthermore,
chloro-
and
ﬂuoro-
hydrocarbons emitted from landﬁlls seriously corrode combustion
engines that utilize landﬁll gas (Dernbach, 1985), deplete the
ozone layer, and cause climate change (Molina and Rowland,
1974; Wallington et al., 1994).
The reported yields of NMOCs varied widely according to the
nature of waste and the experiment condition (Thomas and Barlaz,
1999; Smet et al., 1999; Staley et al., 2006; Wang and Wu, 2008).
The yield of total terpenes from orange wastes was up to
11,000 mg/kg DM (Wang and Wu, 2008), and the NMOC yields of
refuse, paper, yard waste, and food waste were investigated to be
151, 16, 38, and 221 mg C/kg DM, respectively (Staley et al.,
2006). It was also found that NMOC release during aerobic decom-
position of refuse and yard waste was larger than that in anaerobic
systems (Staley et al., 2006). However, Komilis et al. (2004)
detected a VOC yield of food waste as low as 0.33 mg/kg DM under
controlled aerobic conditions, approximately four orders of magni-
tude less than values reported by Staley et al. (2006).
Knox (1990) compared NMOCs released from three main phases
of decomposition, and found that total NMOC concentration ini-
tially increases and then steadily decreases. Moreover, the author
also investigated some categories of NMOC concentrations among
waste degradation processes. Alcohols and halogenated hydrocar-
bons are the main components of NMOCs emitted from young
refuse (Knox, 1990). Deipser and Stegmann (1994) found that the
highest concentrations of volatile chlorinated and ﬂuorinated
hydrocarbons occur during the acid phase in a landﬁll. Kim
(2006) similarly concluded that the proportion of reduced sulfur
compounds is larger in young landﬁlls than in old landﬁlls.

Aromatics and alkanes are the primary components emitted from
middle-aged and old refuses (Knox, 1990).
Sources of NMOCs in landﬁll gas include the anaerobic biodeg-
radation intermediates and the volatilization of hazardous organic
compounds present in MSW (Thomas and Barlaz, 1999). The
decomposition by-products of readily degradable organic matter
are oxygenated compounds, alkanes, and alkenes (Smet et al.,
1999). Aromatics may also be present in food waste because most
aromatics are lipophilic compounds that can be absorbed by lipids
(He et al., 2010). Yard waste, fruit peels, and vegetable leavings are
particularly high in terpenes (Wang and Wu, 2008). According to
Allen et al. (1997), domestic waste releases more alkanes, alcohols,
and ketones than trade waste. Consumer products from the chem-
ical industry contain chlorinated compounds that are directly
volatized in landﬁlls (UK Environment Agency, 2004). Young and
Parker (1983) found that the gas evolved by industrial landﬁlls is
considerably richer in hydrocarbons and solvents, including halo-
carbons, than that from landﬁlls receiving only domestic waste.
Aerobic pretreatment of MSW can not only reduce mass of
waste but improve landﬁll behavior. When aerobically pretreated
MSW (APMSW) is buried in a landﬁll, the leachate pollution load
and the biogas production potential will be diminished (Kuruparan
et al., 2003; Lornage et al., 2007; Scaglia et al., 2010; Tambone
et al., 2011), the stabilization process will be enhanced (Leikam
and Stegmann, 1999; Zach et al., 2000), and the intensity of the
NMOC emissions will be reduced (Zhang et al., in press). To our
best knowledge, however, little information is available on the
effect of organic compositions of APMSW on NMOC characteristics
at different degradation stages. This information is important
because it is helpful for determining the way and the extent of pre-
treatment from perspective of odor control. The objectives of this
study are as follows: (1) to investigate the NMOC emissions from
APMSW with various original organic contents by measuring
NMOC yields and components at two different stages of the anaer-
obic process and by analyzing emission intensities, and (2) to cor-
relate the degraded organic contents with the NMOC yields.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
The original waste A1, approximately 500 kg of MSW was ob-
tained from a landﬁll in Beijing, China. The waste was aerobically
treated to various extents, obtaining ﬁve waste samples of differ-
ent organic compositions (Table 1). The detailed aerobic pretreat-
ment process for the ﬁve wastes is introduced in literature
(Zhang et al., in press).
2.2. Experimental setup
The reactors, made up of high-density polyethylene, each had
an internal diameter of 500 mm and a height of 750 mm (Fig. 1).
The operation modes are shown in Table 2. The reactors R1–R5
were ﬁlled with A1–A5, respectively.
2.3. Sampling and analytical methods
The gas accumulated in the reactors was collected separately at
the end of stage I or II using a previously evacuated SUMMA canis-
ter and then analyzed for the determination of its NMOC composi-
tion. Solid samples were obtained immediately after gas sampling
from the two side samplers and the top of the reactors.
Moisture content (wet basis) was determined by heating the
ground
sample
at 105 C
for
24 h.
Volatile solid
(VS)
was
determined by ashing the dry samples at 550 C to a constant
weight in a mufﬂe furnace (SX2-8-10; NuoJi Instrument Co. Ltd.,
Changzhou, China). Before the organic components were analyzed,
the waste sample was ﬁrst dried at 105 C, and then shredded
using a shredding machine (LK-500; Nongfeng Instrument Co.
Ltd., Zhongshan, China). Protein was determined as Kjeldahl N
times a factor of 6.25 (APHA, 1998). Lipid was determined through
extraction using ether (AOAC, 1990, method no. 920.39). The
remaining organics were called ‘‘others,’’ which were calculated
by subtracting the sum of lipid and protein from VS.
Total carbon (TC) and total nitrogen (TN) were measured using
a carbon–hydrogen–nitrogen analyzer (Equipment CE 440; EAI
USA).

(FID). The measurement setup consisted of a ﬂow controller, a
thermal desorber (Markes International, UK), and a gas chromato-

USEPA standard gases (EPA TO-15) were used for identiﬁcation
of NMOCs. TO-15 (1000  109 V/V) was diluted with high purity
N2 to the concentration 20  109 V/V. The calibration curve using
external standard method was prepared with the diluted standard
gases of six different samplers’ volumes (30, 60, 120, 240, 480, and
720 ml). The r2 of the calibration curve exceeded 0.99. The mean
standard deviations of the ﬁrst and second dimension retention
times of the target compounds were less than 0.6 s and 0.02 s,
respectively. The method detection limits for alkanes, aromatics,
oxygenated, and halohydrocarbon were 4.23, 5.17, 3.41, and
7.80 ng, respectively.
2.4. Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 18.0 for windows
(SPSS Inc., 2009). Multiple linear regression analysis was per-
formed by enter. In the course of enter regression analysis, the
probability values of F were set as 60.05 and P0.1 for entering
and removing a variable, respectively. Correlation and regression
analyses were included to examine NMOCs and the three kinds
of organics, i.e., lipid, protein, and others, measured in the whole
experimental period, i.e., stages I and II, respectively.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Organic degradation
Table 3 presents the fractional degradation of organic matter for
the reactors R1–R5 in stages I and II. In stage I, lipid in R1 and R2,
protein in R5, and others in R3 and R4 degraded to the highest
extent. Others had the highest fractional degradation in stage II
for all reactors except R2, varying from 12.4% to 35.4%. During
the whole experimental period, the leachate pH varied within the
range of 5.1–5.6, suggesting that A1 was still in the hydrolysis
acidiﬁcation stage. Considerable acidiﬁcation inhibits the further
conversion of organics. For the reactors R2–R5, the leachate pH
was above 6.7 and no serious acidiﬁcation occurred during both
stages. The total amounts of VS degradation for R1, R2, R3, R4,
and R5 were 34.8%, 47.2%, 41.1%, 39.8%, and 42.8%, respectively.
Moreover, the compositions of the degraded organics were
investigated (Fig. 2). Others dominated the degraded organics for
all reactors in both stages except for R1, where lipid was the dom-
inant degraded component in stage I. The normalized amount of
degraded protein always overweighed that of lipid in both stages
for reactors R2–R5.
3.2. Yields of NMOCs
The cumulative quantity of NMOCs during stages I and II for
each reactor are presented in Fig. 3. The cumulative weights of
the NMOCs generated in stages I and II were 0.48 and 0.63, 0.13
and 0.17, 0.07 and 0.12, 0.17 and 0.11, and 0.16 and 0.15 mg/kg
DM for R1–R5, respectively. The current results were signiﬁcantly
different from the previously reported values (Thomas and Barlaz,
1999; Staley et al., 2006; Wang and Wu, 2008), probably because of
differences in the experimental scale and characteristics of waste.
The partial NMOC yields in stage II were always larger than in stage
I from R1 to R3, where the whole NMOC yields decreased. In con-
trast, the total NMOC yields slightly increased from R4 to R5, where
the partial NMOC yields in stage I were larger. A possible explana-
tion for this result may be that NMOC yield was affected by the
various degraded components and the conversion paths of organ-
ics. Staley et al. (2006) investigated the NMOCs released from pa-
per, yard waste, and food waste under anaerobic conditions, and

found that NMOC yields from food waste were 5.8 times that of
yard waste and 13.8 times that of paper. The waste A1 initially con-
tained considerably higher lipid than the other wastes. The per-
centage of degraded lipid in the total organics for R1 was higher
than that for the other reactors. Moreover, serious acidiﬁcation in
R1 inhibited microbial activities, and the organic intermediates
were accumulated.
To obtain a comparable situation among the reactors, the NMOC
emissions from R1 to R5 were normalized to emission intensities of
NMOCs by dividing the cumulative NMOC emissions by the quan-
tities of organic matter removed during the anaerobic period (QVS),
which are also shown in Fig. 3. The emission intensities of NMOCs
in stages I and II from R1 to R5 were 4.0 and 4.0, 0.8 and 2.0, 0.9
and 0.9, 2.0 and 1.3, and 3.4 and 1.4 mg/kg QVS, with ratios of
1.01, 0.41, 1.00, 1.59, and 2.50 between them, respectively. In gen-
eral, as the organic content of the original waste became lower, the
proportion of NMOCs became higher at the early stage of anaerobic
degradation. A comparison of Figs. 2 and 3 shows obvious coarse
correlation between NMOC intensities and the degraded amount
of lipid or protein or both in stage I but not in stage II. However,
a simple collection of all the other organics as a uniform ‘‘others’’
group neglects the possible differences among components such
as starch and ﬁbers in releasing NMOCs. Further research is neces-
sary to investigate these details.
3.3. Composition of NMOCs
The NMOCs measured in this study can be grouped into ﬁve cat-
egories: oxygenated compounds (i.e., ketones, alcohols, aldehydes,
acids, and esters), alkanes, alkenes, aromatics, and chlorinated
compounds, similar to the method used by Ran et al. (2009). The
compositions of NMOCs generated from these wastes during stages
I and II are shown in Fig. 4. The dominant NMOC categories were
either oxygenated compounds or alkenes. In both stages, the pro-
portion of oxygenated compounds decreased and that of alkenes
increased from R1 to R5. A comparison of the compositions of
NMOCs in stages I and II showed that, with time, the percentage
of oxygenated and chlorinated compounds decreased, whereas
the percentage of hydrocarbon compounds such as alkanes and al-
kenes increased. The results agree with the conclusions of Knox
(1990) and Deipser and Stegmann (1994). The trends of dominant
NMOC categories from R1 to R5 in stages I and II may be caused by
the fractional degradation of organic matter. The oxygenated
compounds were derived from the decomposition by-products of
readily degradable organic matter. Based on the degradation
efﬁciencies in Table 3, the highest degradation for lipid, protein,
and others in stage I occurred in R1 and R2. For R2–R5 the main de-
graded organic composition was others, as shown in Fig. 2. In stage
II, the domain compositions of the degraded organics for all of the
reactors were others, whereas the fraction of oxygenated com-
pounds in NMOCs was very low (less than 10%), except for R1
(56.5%). A possible explanation for the occurrence of dominant
NMOC categories may be the presence of different types of organic
components, such as starch and ﬁbers, in the waste. The structures
of these components are different in terms of the shape of the bond
that connects their glucose molecules to one another, resulting in
different degradation rates. Starch, as a kind of readily degradable
organic matter, is degraded earlier and easier than ﬁber. Therefore,
the main degraded components of others were ﬁber for R2–R5 and
starch for R1 in stage II.
Nagata (2003) investigated the odor threshold distribution for
NMOCs. The author found that the odor threshold is 10–100 ppb
for oxygenated compounds, 100 ppb to 1 ppm for hydrocarbons,
and 1–10 ppm for chlorinated compounds. Humans are normally
more sensitive to NMOCs with lower odor thresholds. With a
decrease in organic contents of initial wastes and with the degra-
dations, the NMOC yields decreased and the percentage of oxygen-
ated compounds in NMOCs decreased. Thus, the odor may be
weakened, to the point that it is less perceptible for humans.
The main components of the total 89 NMOC species in stages I
and II were also investigated. Fig. 5 shows the individual compo-
nents whose mass contents are more than 5% of total NMOCs
during stage I or II. As organic contents of initial wastes decreased,
the mass contents of 2-butanone, ethyl acetate, ethanol, and ace-
tone in stage I and the mass content of phenol in stage II declined,
while the mass contents of pentane and 1,2-dichloroethane in
stage I and the mass contents of hexadecane in stage II increased.
3.4. Correlation analysis between organics and NMOCs
The correlation analysis showed that lipid had signiﬁcant corre-
lation with NMOCs in stages I and II. In comparison, protein had
signiﬁcant correlation with NMOCs only in stage I, and neither
with others. Table 4 summarizes the correlations between the de-
graded lipid (X1) and protein (X2), and the released NMOCs (Y) by
enter regression analysis. Based on the partial F test and the value
of R, strong linear relationships were found between NMOCs and
lipid and/or protein. The effect of lipid on NMOC quantity probably
lasted longer than that of protein. Therefore, controlling the lipid
and protein contents of MSW for landﬁll disposal can be an effec-
tive option for odor reduction, especially for some Asian countries

4. Conclusions
The yields and compositions of NMOCs from ﬁve kinds of
APMSW with various organic contents were investigated in the
processes of anaerobic degradation. With total VS degradation of
34.8–47.2%, the emission intensities of NMOCs from R1 to R5 were
8.0, 2.8, 1.8, 3.3, and 4.8 mg/kg QVS, with ratios of 1.01, 0.41, 1.00,
1.59, and 2.50, respectively, between stages I and II. The dominant
categories of NMOCs changed from oxygenated compounds (e.g.
2-butanone, ethyl acetate, ethanol, acetone and phenol) to alkanes
(e.g. Hexadecane and pentane) when the readily degradable organ-
ic content of waste decreased. Based on the correlation analysis,
lipid and protein have signiﬁcant correlations with NMOC quan-
tity, and the effect of lipid on NMOC emission lasts longer than that
of protein. Therefore, controlling the lipid and protein contents of
initial MSW will be helpful in reducing odor in landﬁlls.
